newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY FARMERS RENEW BLOCKADE AHEAD OF GOVT TALKS.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY FARMERS RENEW BLOCKADE AHEAD OF GOVT TALKS.

text.p: Hungary's government faced new roadblocks on Wednesday as proesting farmers go beyond tax complaints and demand an overhaul of the country's battered agriculture.
"The government just won't listen to reason," Huba Kozma, head of farmers' association MAGOSZ, told Reuters. "They will only bow to pressure".

Last week, a series of roadblocks slowed down traffic in central Hungary, in a protest against increased taxes by an ad-hoc group of farmers from Kiskoros, on the Hungarian Plain, who have since formed their own organisation, MTESZ.
Their leader, Gyula Kosa, claims to represent the interests of millions of Hungarians who work the land, but there are about a dozen such organisations, often with conflicting goals.
Last Tuesday, the government accepted most changes the Kiskoros protesters asked for, but they now seem to want more out of Wednesday's new round of talks with government officials.
However, Kosa refused to say what exactly their new claims would be, when he meets Prime Minister Gyula Horn, Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy and Agriculture Minister Frigyes Nagy.
"It would be premature to disclose our position ahead of the talks," he said.

Their protest, was due to start at 0800 GMT and is scheduled to last until agreement with the government or in case of failure until the end of next week, and, if necessary, will be followed by further action by MAGOSZ.

The MAGOSZ protest is due to start on March 10 and is designed to give weight to a 12-point list of demands, including a government guarantee of an 8 to 10 percent profit margin on farming, protective import duties and the suspension of this year's new tax regulations.
Agriculture Minister Nagy is expected to deliver the draft of a comprehensive medium-term agricultural programme on Thursday, which the government says would deal with most of farmers' demands.
Both MAGOSZ and MTESZ said, however, that they were not even shown the draft.
"I have no idea what it will contain," Kosa said.
Before coming to power in 1994, Hungary's Socialist Party promised to streamline the country's agriculture but have yet to make significant headway.

Since the collapse of communism, food consumption, livestock and agricultural productivity has been in steady decline, a fact recognized by Nagy, the fifth person to hold the agriculture portfolio in six years.
"Agriculture is in crisis, but not in an impossible situation," he said last month.

Nagy and the government face a difficult balancing act as they try to keep a tight rein on costs in the run-up to eventual European Union membership, while avoiding further upsetting farmers ahead of general elections in 1998.
The task is further complicated by farmers' reluctance to provide even the most basic information about their incomes, the size of holdings or crops.
Prime Minister Gyula Horn said on Tuesday that in 1995, only 13,000 of Hungary's 1.5 million farmers submitted an income tax return.
